cards.trick: Sort by width ascending and by height DESCENDING on ties, so equal widths cannot chain. Then find the longest strictly increasing subsequence of heights with the patience-sorting tails array and binary search.

cards.name: Score After Flipping Matrix
cards.trick: The leftmost bit is worth the most, so flip every row whose first cell is 0. Then for each other column flip it if it has more 0s than 1s, so add max(ones, zeros) * 2^(n - 1 - j) per column.

cards.name: Score of a String
cards.trick: Sum the absolute differences of ASCII values of each adjacent pair of chars in one pass.

cards.name: Search in a Sorted Array of Unknown Size
cards.trick: Find the bounds by doubling: set r = 1 and double it while reader.get(r) < target. Then do normal binary search on [r / 2, r]. Out-of-range reads return a huge value, so they act like +infinity.

cards.name: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
cards.time: O(log n) average, O(n) worst (many duplicates)
cards.trick: Standard rotated binary search, but when nums[l] == nums[mid] == nums[r] you cannot tell which half is sorted, so shrink l++ and r--. Otherwise find the sorted half and check whether target lies in it.

cards.name: Search Insert Position
cards.trick: Lower-bound binary search: find the first index with nums[i] >= target. Use l < r with r = n, mid = (l + r) / 2, move r = mid when nums[mid] >= target, else l = mid + 1.

cards.name: Search Suggestions System
cards.time: O(n log n + L log n) (n products, L = search word length, ignoring string compares)
cards.trick: Sort products. For each prefix of the search word, binary search the lower bound of that prefix and take up to 3 consecutive products that still start with it. The start pointer only moves right. (Trie storing top 3 per node is the alternative.)

cards.name: Seat Reservation Manager
cards.trick: Keep a counter for the next never-used seat plus a min-heap of unreserved (released) seats. reserve() pops the heap if non-empty, else increments the counter. unreserve(x) pushes x onto the heap.

cards.name: Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination
cards.trick: BFS counting edges (not time) and keep the two smallest distinct edge counts per node: dist1 and dist2. Take dist2 of node n, then convert edges to time by simulating each step through the traffic signal (wait if the light is red).

cards.name: Sentence Screen Fitting
cards.trick: Join words as 'a b c ' into one string s and keep a pointer pos into the infinite repetition. Per row pos += cols; if s[pos % len] is a space pos++, else back up while the previous char is not a space. Answer is pos / len.

cards.name: Sentence Similarity
cards.trick: Lengths must match. Put each similar pair in a hash set (both orders). Word i matches if the words are equal or the pair is in the set. Similarity is not transitive, so no union-find.

cards.name: Sentence Similarity II
cards.trick: Similarity is transitive, so union-find over words: union each pair, then compare word i of both sentences by equality or same root. Lengths must match. (DFS per word pair is slower.)

cards.name: Sentence Similarity III
cards.trick: Split into words. Advance a pointer over the matching prefix words and another over the matching suffix words. Similar iff prefix + suffix matches cover the whole shorter sentence.

cards.name: Separate Black and White Balls
cards.trick: Every '0' must pass every '1' to its left, and swaps are adjacent. Scan once keeping the count of '1's seen; on each '0' add that count to the answer.

cards.name: Sequence Reconstruction
cards.trick: Topological sort (Kahn) on edges between adjacent elements of each sequence. The original is the unique shortest supersequence iff the queue holds exactly one node at every step and the resulting order equals nums.

cards.name: Sequential Digits
cards.trick: Every sequential-digit number is a substring of '123456789'. For each length from len(low) to len(high), slide a window over that string, convert and keep those within [low, high]. Output is already sorted.

cards.name: Serialize and Deserialize N-ary Tree
cards.trick: Preorder, writing each node as its value followed by its child count. Deserialize with a recursive reader: read val, read k, then build k children recursively. The count replaces null markers.

cards.name: Set Mismatch
cards.trick: Use the array as its own visited map. For each x flip the sign of nums[abs(x) - 1]; if it is already negative, abs(x) is the duplicate. The index that is still positive afterwards, plus 1, is the missing number.

cards.name: Shift 2D Grid
cards.trick: Treat the grid as a flat list of length m * n. Cell (i, j) has index i * n + j and moves to (idx + k) % (m * n), which maps back to row idx / n and column idx % n. No simulation of k shifts.

cards.name: Shifting Letters II
cards.trick: Difference array: for each shift [l, r, d] add +1 or -1 at l and the opposite at r + 1. Prefix sum gives each char's net shift. Apply ((c - 'a' + shift) % 26 + 26) % 26.

cards.name: Shortest Bridge
cards.trick: DFS the first island, marking it visited and pushing all its cells into a queue. Then multi-source BFS outward over water; the level at which you first touch the other island is the number of flips.

cards.name: Shortest Common Supersequence
cards.trick: Build the LCS dp table of the two strings, then walk back from (m, n): on a match emit the char once and go diagonal, otherwise emit the char from the string you step away from. Append what remains, reverse. Length = m + n - LCS.

cards.name: Shortest Distance After Road Addition Queries I
cards.trick: Keep an adjacency list starting with the chain i -> i + 1. After each added edge u -> v, run a BFS from 0 to n - 1 and record the distance. Constraints are small enough that BFS per query is the intended solution.

cards.name: Shortest Distance From All Buildings
cards.trick: BFS from every building (not from every empty cell), adding distances into a total[][] grid and counting how many buildings reach each cell. Answer is the min total over cells reached by all k buildings, else -1.

cards.name: Shortest Distance to Target Color
cards.trick: Only 3 colors, so precompute left[i][c] = nearest index <= i with color c and right[i][c] = nearest index >= i with color c in two sweeps. Each query is the min of the two distances. (Per-color index lists plus binary search is O(q log n).)

cards.name: Shortest Palindrome
cards.trick: Find the longest palindromic prefix of s using KMP failure function on s + '#' + reverse(s). Prepend the reverse of the remaining suffix. (Rolling hash on prefix vs reverse also works.)

cards.name: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
cards.trick: BFS from (0, 0) over 8 directions through 0-cells, counting cells on the path (start counts as 1). Return -1 if either corner is blocked. BFS gives the shortest path since all steps cost 1.

cards.name: Shortest Path to Get Food
cards.trick: Multi-step BFS from the '*' start through non-obstacle cells; return the step count the first time you reach a '#'. Mark cells visited when enqueued. Return -1 if the queue empties.

cards.name: Shortest Path With Alternating Colors
cards.trick: BFS over states (node, color of the last edge used). Keep separate red and blue adjacency lists, start with both (0, red) and (0, blue) at distance 0, and take the min distance over the two colors per node.

cards.name: Shortest Subarray to Be Removed to Make Array Sorted
cards.trick: Find the longest non-decreasing prefix and suffix. If the whole array is sorted return 0. Start with removing the middle or all of one side, then two-pointer merge: for each prefix end i advance j in the suffix while arr[j] < arr[i]; minimize j - i - 1.

cards.name: Shortest Subarray With OR at Least K II
cards.trick: OR is not subtractable, so keep a count per bit position inside the window. Add a number by incrementing its set bits, shrink from the left while the OR (bits with count > 0) is >= k, and track the min length.

cards.name: Shortest Subarray With Sum at Least K
cards.trick: Negatives break a plain sliding window. Use prefix sums and a monotonic increasing deque of indices: pop from the front while prefix[i] - prefix[front] >= k (record length), pop from the back while prefix[back] >= prefix[i], then push i.

cards.name: Shortest Way to Form String
cards.trick: Greedily take the longest subsequence of source per pass over target. Precompute next[i][c] = next index >= i where char c appears in source, so each target char is matched in O(1). Return -1 if a char is missing. (Plain two pointers is O(m * n).)

cards.name: Shortest Word Distance
cards.trick: One pass tracking the most recent index of word1 and of word2. Whenever you see either word, update its index and, if both are set, update the min of abs(i1 - i2).

cards.name: Shortest Word Distance II
cards.time: O(n) to build, O(a + b) per query (a, b = occurrence counts)
cards.trick: Constructor builds a hash map from word to its sorted list of indices. Each query merges the two sorted lists with two pointers, always advancing the pointer at the smaller index, and tracks the min gap.

cards.name: Shortest Word Distance III
cards.trick: Same one-pass idea, but word1 may equal word2. When they are equal compare each occurrence with the previous occurrence of that same word: take the distance to the last index first, then overwrite it.

cards.name: Shuffle the Array
cards.space: O(n) (O(1) extra by packing two values per int)
cards.trick: For i in 0..n-1 set res[2i] = nums[i] and res[2i + 1] = nums[i + n]. In place: store nums[i + n] in the high bits of nums[i] (values <= 1000, use 10 bits) and unpack from the back.

cards.name: Sign of the Product of an Array
cards.trick: Do not multiply (overflow). Return 0 immediately if any element is 0; otherwise count negatives and return -1 if the count is odd, else 1.

cards.name: Similar RGB Color
cards.trick: The shorthand '#abc' means each channel is a multiple of 17 (0x11). Split the color into 3 channels and independently round each to the nearest multiple of 17 (round(c / 17) * 17). Channels are independent, so minimizing each minimizes the total.

cards.name: Simplify Path
cards.trick: Split on '/'. Skip empty parts and '.', pop the stack on '..' (if non-empty), push anything else. Join with '/' and prefix a leading '/'.

cards.name: Single Element in a Sorted Array
cards.trick: Before the single element pairs start at even indices; after it they start at odd indices. Binary search on mid made even (mid -= mid % 2): if nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1] the single is to the right, else it is at mid or left.

cards.name: Single Number III
cards.trick: XOR everything to get a ^ b. Isolate any set bit with diff = x & -x; a and b differ at that bit. Split the numbers by that bit and XOR each group separately to get a and b.

cards.name: Single-Row Keyboard
cards.trick: Map each key to its index, then sum abs(index[word[i]] - index[word[i - 1]]) starting from position 0.

cards.name: Single-Threaded CPU
cards.trick: Sort tasks by enqueue time (keeping original index). Min-heap keyed on (processing time, index). At the current time push all tasks that have arrived, pop one to run and advance time; if the heap is empty jump time to the next enqueue time.

cards.name: Sliding Puzzle
cards.trick: BFS over board states encoded as 6-char strings, starting from the given board and stopping at '123450'. Precompute which positions each index of the 0 can swap with. Visited set avoids repeats; return -1 if the target is unreachable.

cards.name: Smallest Common Region
cards.trick: Map each region to its parent. Add region1 and all its ancestors to a set, then walk up from region2 until you hit a region in the set. That is the lowest common ancestor.

cards.name: Smallest Greater Multiple Made of Two Digits
cards.trick: Generate numbers using only the two digits in increasing order (BFS or DFS with digit order min, max) up to the 32-bit limit (at most 10 digits, about 2^10 numbers). Return the first that is > k and divisible by k, else -1.

cards.name: Smallest Range Covering Elements From K Lists
cards.trick: Min-heap holding one element from each list, tracking the current max. The range is [heap min, max]. Pop the min, record the range if smaller, push the next element from that list and update max. Stop when a list runs out.

cards.name: Smallest Rectangle Enclosing Black Pixels
cards.time: O(m log n + n log m)
cards.trick: Black pixels are connected, so each row or column containing black is contiguous around the given pixel. Binary search the top, bottom, left and right boundaries: for a column test whether any row has a black pixel. Area = (right - left) * (bottom - top). (DFS/BFS is O(m * n).)

cards.name: Smallest String Starting From Leaf
cards.trick: DFS carrying the path string built by prepending each node's letter (so it reads leaf to root). At every leaf compare to the best string so far and keep the smaller. A prefix that is shorter counts as smaller.

cards.name: Snakes and Ladders
cards.trick: BFS over squares 1..n^2, each move tries rolls 1 to 6. Convert a square number to (row, col) with the boustrophedon layout (rows from the bottom, alternating direction). If the board cell is not -1 jump to it once; return the level when you reach n^2.

cards.name: Solving Questions With Brainpower
cards.trick: DP from the right: dp[i] = max(dp[i + 1] (skip), points[i] + dp[min(n, i + brainpower[i] + 1)] (solve)). Answer is dp[0]. Going right to left means the future state is already computed.

cards.name: Sort an Array
cards.trick: Needs a guaranteed O(n log n), so use merge sort (or heap sort for O(1) space), not a naive quicksort that degrades to O(n^2). Values are bounded, so counting sort O(n + range) also works.

cards.name: Sort Array by Increasing Frequency
cards.trick: Count frequencies with a hash map, then sort with key (frequency ascending, value descending). The tie-break on value descending is the easy part to forget.

cards.name: Sort Array By Parity
cards.trick: Pointers at both ends. If left is odd and right is even swap them; advance left while it is even and move right back while it is odd. In place, one pass.

cards.name: Sort Characters By Frequency
cards.trick: Count chars, then bucket sort: bucket[freq] holds chars with that frequency. Walk buckets from highest frequency down, appending each char freq times. (Sorting or a max-heap is O(n log k).)

cards.name: Sort Colors
cards.trick: Dutch national flag with low, mid, high. 0 at mid: swap with low and advance both. 1: advance mid. 2: swap with high and decrement high only (the swapped-in value is unchecked).

cards.name: Sort Features by Popularity
cards.time: O(F log F + total words in responses)
cards.trick: For each response split into a set of words so a feature counts once per response. Count popularity per feature, then stable sort feature indices by count descending (ties keep original order).

cards.name: Sort Linked List Already Sorted Using Absolute Values
cards.trick: The list is sorted by absolute value, so negatives appear in reverse order of what we need. Walk with prev/cur; whenever cur is negative, unlink it and insert it at the head. No sorting needed.

cards.name: Sort List
cards.space: O(log n) (O(1) with bottom-up merge sort)
cards.trick: Merge sort on a linked list. Split at the middle using slow/fast pointers (cut slow.next), sort both halves recursively, then merge two sorted lists. Linked lists merge without extra arrays.

cards.name: Sort the Jumbled Numbers
cards.time: O(n log n + n * d) (d = digits per number)
cards.trick: Compute each number's mapped value digit by digit (handle 0 as a single digit). Then stable sort the original numbers by mapped value, so equal mapped values keep their original order.

cards.name: Sort the People
cards.trick: Pair each name with its height and sort the pairs by height descending (or sort indices by heights), then return the names.

cards.name: Sort Transformed Array
cards.trick: f(x) = a*x^2 + b*x + c is a parabola, so extremes are at the ends of the sorted input. Two pointers from both ends: if a >= 0 the larger value goes to the back of the result (fill from the end), if a < 0 the smaller value goes to the front. a == 0 behaves like a >= 0.

cards.name: Sparse Matrix Multiplication
cards.time: O(m * k * n) worst case, much less when sparse
cards.trick: Loop i, k and skip when A[i][k] == 0; only then loop j (skipping B[k][j] == 0) and add A[i][k] * B[k][j] to C[i][j]. Or store only the non-zero entries per row as lists and multiply those.

cards.name: Special Array I
cards.trick: Every adjacent pair must have different parity. Return false if any nums[i] % 2 == nums[i + 1] % 2.

cards.name: Special Array With X Elements Greater Than or Equal X
cards.trick: Counting array of size n + 1 where cnt[min(num, n)]++. Scan x from n down keeping a running suffix sum; the first x where suffix count == x is the answer, else -1. (Sort and binary search is O(n log n).)

cards.name: Spiral Matrix II
cards.trick: Four boundaries top, bottom, left, right. Fill the top row left to right, right column downward, bottom row right to left, left column upward with an incrementing counter, then shrink each boundary by 1 and repeat.

cards.name: Spiral Matrix III
cards.trick: Walk the spiral outward from the start with step lengths 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, ... and direction order east, south, west, north. Record a cell only when it is inside the grid; stop once m * n cells are recorded. The walk may leave the grid and come back.

cards.name: Spiral Matrix IV
cards.trick: Fill the matrix with -1, then walk the spiral (right, down, left, up) writing list values. Turn clockwise when the next cell is out of bounds or already filled; stop when the list ends.

cards.name: Split a String Into the Max Number of Unique Substrings
cards.trick: Backtrack over cut positions with a set of substrings already used. Try every end for the next piece, skip if it is already used. Prune when used count + remaining chars <= best so far.

cards.name: Split Array Largest Sum
cards.trick: Binary search the answer between max(nums) and sum(nums). For a candidate cap, greedily pack elements into subarrays and count them; if count <= k the cap is feasible so search lower, else higher. (DP is O(n^2 * k).)

cards.name: Split Array With Equal Sum
cards.trick: Prefix sums. Fix the middle cut j. For i < j, if sum(0..i-1) == sum(i+1..j-1) add that sum to a set. Then for k > j, if sum(j+1..k-1) == sum(k+1..n-1) and that sum is in the set, return true.

cards.name: Split Array With Same Average
cards.trick: Need a subset of size k with sum = total * k / n, so only try k where total * k % n == 0. dp[k] = set of reachable sums using k elements, built item by item. (Meet in the middle is O(n * 2^(n/2)).)

cards.name: Split BST
cards.trick: Recurse on the BST property. If root.val <= target, root joins the small tree: split root.right and reattach its small part as root.right. Otherwise mirror it on the left side.

cards.name: Split Concatenated Strings
cards.trick: Replace every string with the larger of itself and its reverse. Then try each string as the cut point in both orientations, joining the rest in order, and take the best rotation of the resulting loop.

cards.name: Split Linked List in Parts
cards.trick: Count length n. Each part gets n // k nodes and the first n % k parts get one extra. Walk each part, then set the last node's next to null to cut it.

cards.name: Splitting a String Into Descending Consecutive Values
cards.trick: Try every first piece (not the whole string), then each next piece is forced to equal prev - 1, so just check the next substring matches. Prune as soon as a value mismatches. Strip leading zeros by parsing as ints.

cards.name: Sqrt(x)
cards.trick: Binary search the answer in [0, x]. Compare mid * mid to x and keep the largest mid with mid * mid <= x. (Newton's method converges in O(log log x).)

cards.name: Squares of a Sorted Array
cards.trick: Largest square is at one of the two ends because of negatives. Pointers at both ends, write the larger square into the result from the back, and move that pointer inward.

cards.name: Squirrel Simulation
cards.trick: Every nut costs 2 * dist(nut, tree) except the first one, which costs dist(squirrel, nut) + dist(nut, tree). Total = sum of 2 * dist(nut, tree) + min over nuts of (dist(squirrel, nut) - dist(nut, tree)).

cards.name: Step-By-Step Directions From a Binary Tree Node to Another
cards.trick: Record the root-to-start and root-to-dest paths as strings of L and R. Strip their common prefix (that is the LCA), turn every remaining start step into U, then append the remaining dest path.

cards.name: Stepping Numbers
cards.time: O(S) (S = count of stepping numbers up to high, about O(2^d) for d digits)
cards.trick: Build numbers digit by digit: from last digit d, append d - 1 and d + 1 (when in 0-9). Start from 1-9, stop a branch once the value exceeds high, and count values >= low. Count 0 separately if low is 0.

cards.name: Stickers to Spell Word
cards.time: O(2^T * S * T) (T = target length, S = stickers)
cards.trick: Bitmask DP over which target letters are already covered, memoized. Only try stickers that contain the first uncovered letter, which removes duplicate orderings and prunes branching.

cards.name: Stone Game
cards.trick: Even number of piles and odd total, so Alice can force taking all even-index piles or all odd-index piles, and one of the two sets is strictly larger. Always return true. (Interval DP is O(n^2).)

cards.name: Stone Game II
cards.trick: dp[i][M] = most stones the current player gets from piles i onward with limit M. Try taking X in 1..2M, then dp = suffixSum[i] - (best the opponent gets at dp[i + X][max(M, X)]). Suffix sums make it zero-sum.

cards.name: Stone Game III
cards.trick: dp[i] = best score difference (me minus opponent) from pile i on. dp[i] = max over k in 1..3 of sum(piles[i..i+k-1]) - dp[i+k]. Only the last 3 values are needed. Answer by sign of dp[0].

cards.name: String Compression
cards.trick: Read pointer scans runs of equal chars, write pointer overwrites in place. Write the char, then if the run length > 1 write its digits one char at a time (so 12 becomes '1','2'). Return the write index.

cards.name: String Compression II
cards.trick: dp[i][k] = min encoded length from index i with k deletions left. Either delete s[i], or keep it as the head of a group, scan right keeping equal chars and deleting different ones, and add the run-length cost (1, 2, 3 or 4 digits).

cards.name: String Matching in an Array
cards.time: O(n^2 * L) (n words, L = max word length)
cards.trick: For each word check whether it is a substring of any other word, using KMP for the check so each test is linear. (Simple built-in substring search is O(n^2 * L^2) worst case but fine for the limits.)

cards.name: String Transforms Into Another String
cards.trick: If str1 == str2 return true. Map each char of str1 to its target and fail on any conflict. If str2 uses all 26 letters there is no spare letter to break a cycle, so return false. Otherwise true.

cards.name: Strings Differ by One Character
cards.time: O(n * m) (n words of length m)
cards.trick: For each column i, hash every word with position i wildcarded and look for a repeat in a set. Use a rolling hash from prefix and suffix hashes so each wildcard hash is O(1). (Building masked strings is O(n * m^2).)

cards.name: Strobogrammatic Number
cards.trick: Pointers at both ends. Each pair must be a valid rotation pair: 0-0, 1-1, 8-8, 6-9, 9-6. The middle char of an odd length must be 0, 1 or 8, which the same check covers when i == j.

cards.name: Strobogrammatic Number II
cards.trick: Build from the middle outward: helper(n) takes helper(n - 2) and wraps each result with the pairs 00, 11, 69, 88, 96. Base cases are '' and 0, 1, 8. Do not use the 00 wrap at the outermost level (no leading zero).

cards.name: Strobogrammatic Number III
cards.trick: Generate strobogrammatic numbers for each length from len(low) to len(high) with the middle-outward builder. Count those whose value is within [low, high], comparing as strings only when length equals len(low) or len(high).

cards.name: Student Attendance Record II
cards.trick: State = (absences 0 or 1, trailing lates 0 to 2), so 6 states rolled day by day. Present resets lates, Late increments lates, Absent needs absences == 0. Mod 1e9+7. (Matrix exponentiation is O(log n).)

cards.name: Subarray Product Less Than K
cards.trick: Window with a running product. Shrink from the left while product >= k, then add r - l + 1 new subarrays ending at r. Handle k <= 1 up front by returning 0.

cards.name: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
cards.trick: Two equal prefix sums mod k bound a divisible subarray. Count prefix remainders in a map seeded with {0: 1}, and add the count of the current remainder before incrementing. Normalize negatives with ((x % k) + k) % k.

cards.name: Subarrays With K Different Integers
cards.trick: Exactly k = atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1). atMost(k) is a sliding window with a count map that adds r - l + 1 per right end after shrinking until distinct count <= k.

cards.name: Subsequence of Size K With the Largest Even Sum
cards.trick: Sort descending and take the top k. If the sum is odd, fix parity with the cheapest swap: smallest odd inside for largest even outside, or smallest even inside for largest odd outside. Take the better one, or return -1 if neither exists.

cards.name: Substrings That Begin and End With the Same Letter
cards.trick: A letter appearing f times gives f * (f + 1) / 2 substrings. Or in one pass: increment count[ch] first, then add count[ch] to the answer.

cards.name: Subtree Removal Game With Fibonacci Tree
cards.trick: Sprague-Grundy on the Fibonacci tree: g(n) = (g(n-1) + 1) XOR (g(n-2) + 1). The first player loses exactly when g(n) == 0, which is periodic, so return n % 6 != 1.

cards.name: Successful Pairs of Spells and Potions
cards.trick: Sort potions. For each spell binary search the first potion >= ceil(success / spell); the pair count is m minus that index. (Sorting both and using two pointers also works.)

cards.name: Sum of Absolute Differences in a Sorted Array
cards.trick: Sorted, so for index i the sum is nums[i] * i - leftSum + (rightSum - nums[i] * (n - 1 - i)). Keep a running prefix sum and derive the suffix from the total.

cards.name: Sum of All Subset XOR Totals
cards.trick: Every bit set in any element appears in exactly half of the subsets. So the answer is (OR of all nums) * 2^(n - 1). (Backtracking over subsets is O(2^n).)

cards.name: Sum of Digits in the Minimum Number
cards.trick: Find the minimum, sum its digits, and return 1 if that sum is even, else 0.

cards.name: Sum of Prefix Scores of Strings
cards.trick: Insert every word into a trie, incrementing a pass-through count at each node. A word's score is the sum of the counts along its path, so a second walk per word gives the answer.

cards.name: Sum Of Special Evenly-Spaced Elements In Array
cards.trick: Sqrt decomposition, offline. For step y >= sqrt(n), brute force (at most sqrt(n) terms). For small y, group queries by y and build suffix sums with step y: s[i] = nums[i] + s[i + y]. Mod 1e9+7.

cards.name: Sum of Square Numbers
cards.trick: Two pointers a = 0 and b = floor(sqrt(c)). If a^2 + b^2 is too small increase a, too big decrease b. Use a long to avoid overflow.

cards.name: Sum of Subarray Minimums
cards.trick: Monotonic stack. For each i find the distance to the previous strictly smaller element and the next smaller-or-equal element (asymmetric to avoid double counting). Contribution = arr[i] * left * right. Mod 1e9+7.

cards.name: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
cards.trick: DFS carrying the number so far as cur * 10 + node.val. At a leaf add cur to the total. (Morris traversal gets O(1) space.)

cards.name: Swap Nodes in Pairs
cards.trick: Dummy head and a prev pointer. For each pair (a, b) do prev.next = b, a.next = b.next, b.next = a, then move prev to a. Stop when fewer than two nodes remain.

cards.name: Swapping Nodes in a Linked List
cards.trick: Advance a pointer k - 1 steps to the kth node from the start. Then start a second pointer at head and move both until the first hits the tail, so the second sits at the kth from the end. Swap their values.

cards.name: Symmetric Tree
cards.trick: isMirror(a, b): both null is true, one null or different values is false, else compare a.left with b.right and a.right with b.left.

cards.name: Synonymous Sentences
cards.time: O(k^w * w) (w = words in text, k = max synonym group size)
cards.trick: Union-find (or DFS) merges synonym pairs into groups, since synonymy is transitive. Sort each group, then backtrack over the words of the sentence, trying each group member. Output is bounded by the number of sentences.

cards.name: Take Gifts From the Richest Pile
cards.trick: Max heap of piles. k times pop the largest, push floor(sqrt(it)). Sum what remains. Heapify in O(n) first.

cards.name: Take K of Each Character From Left and Right
cards.trick: Taking from both ends means the untouched part is a middle window. Return -1 if the total count of any of a, b, c is < k. Then find the longest window whose removal still leaves >= k of each char; answer = n - longest.

cards.name: Ternary Expression Parser
cards.trick: Scan right to left pushing chars. When the stack top is '?' the current char is a condition: pop '?', the true value, ':' and the false value, then push the chosen one. The stack ends with the result.

cards.name: Text Justification
cards.trick: Greedily pack as many words as fit with one space between. Spread the extra spaces across the gaps with the leftover going to the leftmost gaps. The last line and single-word lines are left-justified and padded on the right.

cards.name: The Earliest Moment When Everyone Become Friends
cards.trick: Sort logs by timestamp and union the two people in each. When the number of components reaches 1, return that timestamp. Return -1 if it never does.

cards.name: The k-th Lexicographical String of All Happy Strings of Length n
cards.trick: There are 3 * 2^(n-1) happy strings. Pick each character by counting: with the first char chosen, each later choice splits the rest into groups of size 2^(remaining - 1), so k picks the branch directly. Return '' if k exceeds the total. (Plain backtracking is O(k * n).)

cards.name: The Maze
cards.trick: BFS or DFS where nodes are stopping points. From a stop, roll each direction until the next cell is a wall, and enqueue that stop if unvisited. Reaching the destination as a stopping point means true.

cards.name: The Maze II
cards.trick: Dijkstra over stopping points. Edge weight = number of cells rolled in one direction until blocked. Relax each of 4 rolls from the popped stop and return dist[destination] or -1.

cards.name: The Maze III
cards.time: O(m * n * (m + n + log(m * n))) (ignoring path string compares)
cards.trick: Dijkstra on (distance, path string), so ties on distance break by lexicographically smallest path. While rolling, stop immediately if you pass the hole, since the ball falls in. Return the path when the hole is popped, else 'impossible'.

cards.name: The Most Similar Path in a Graph
cards.time: O(L * (n + m)) (L = target path length, n cities, m roads)
cards.trick: dp[i][v] = min edit distance of a path of length i ending at city v, where the cost is 1 if name[v] != target[i]. Take the min over neighbors u of dp[i-1][u], store parents, then walk back from the best end city to rebuild the path.

cards.name: The Number of Beautiful Subsets
cards.trick: Group values by residue mod k and sort distinct values; only values differing by exactly k conflict, so each group is a chain. Per chain do take/skip DP where taking a value with count c has 2^c - 1 choices. Multiply chains and subtract 1 for the empty set. (Backtracking with a count map is O(2^n).)

cards.name: The Number of the Smallest Unoccupied Chair
cards.trick: Sort friends by arrival. Min heap of free chair numbers (0..n-1) and a min heap of (leave time, chair). Before seating each friend, release every chair whose leave time <= arrival, then pop the smallest free chair.

cards.name: Time Needed to Buy Tickets
cards.trick: No simulation needed. Person i contributes min(tickets[i], tickets[k]) if i <= k, and min(tickets[i], tickets[k] - 1) if i > k, because they stand behind k in the final round. Sum these.

cards.name: Time Needed to Inform All Employees
cards.trick: Build manager -> subordinates lists. DFS from the head: time(node) = informTime[node] + max(time(child)). The answer is the longest root-to-leaf sum of informTime.

cards.name: Time Taken to Cross the Door
cards.trick: Simulate second by second with two queues (enter, exit). Priority: if the door was used last second, same direction as then wins; if it was idle, exit wins. If both queues are empty, jump time to the next arrival and reset the state to idle.

cards.name: Toss Strange Coins
cards.trick: dp[j] = probability of exactly j heads so far, starting with dp[0] = 1. For each coin p update j downward: dp[j] = dp[j] * (1 - p) + dp[j - 1] * p. Answer is dp[target].

cards.name: Transpose Matrix
cards.trick: Allocate an n x m result and set res[c][r] = matrix[r][c]. Matrix may be non-square so in-place swapping does not work in general.

cards.name: Trapping Rain Water II
cards.trick: Min heap seeded with all border cells (the walls). Pop the lowest wall, visit unvisited neighbors: water += max(0, wall - neighbor), and push the neighbor with height max(neighbor, wall). Water level is always set by the lowest boundary.

cards.name: Tree Diameter
cards.trick: Double BFS: BFS from any node to find the farthest node a, then BFS from a; the farthest distance is the diameter in edges. (One DFS returning heights, with diameter = top two child heights summed, also works.)

cards.name: Triangle
cards.trick: Go bottom up with a 1-D array seeded from the last row. For each row above, dp[j] = tri[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j + 1]). dp[0] at the end is the answer.

cards.name: Trim a Binary Search Tree
cards.trick: Recurse. If root.val < low, the answer is trim(root.right). If root.val > high, it is trim(root.left). Otherwise trim both children and keep the root.

cards.name: Tuple With Same Product
cards.trick: Count how many pairs give each product in a hash map. A product with c pairs makes c * (c - 1) / 2 pair-of-pairs, each giving 8 tuples (orderings). Elements are distinct, so no overlap problems.

cards.name: Two City Scheduling
cards.trick: Sort by cost[0] - cost[1]. The first half (most savings going to A) fly to city A and the rest to city B.

cards.name: Two Sum BSTs
cards.trick: Two pointers over sorted order: an ascending inorder iterator on tree 1 and a descending reverse-inorder iterator on tree 2, each a stack. Sum too small advance the first, too big advance the second. (Hash set of one tree is O(n) space.)

cards.name: Two Sum III - Data Structure Design
cards.trick: Hash map of value -> count. In find, for each key check whether target - key exists; if target - key == key it needs count >= 2. (Keeping a sorted list makes add O(n) and find O(n) with two pointers.)

cards.name: Two Sum Less Than K
cards.trick: Sort, then pointers at both ends. If sum < k record the best and move left up, otherwise move right down. Return -1 if no pair was recorded. (Counting sort works as values <= 1000.)

cards.name: Ugly Number
cards.trick: If n <= 0 return false. Divide out all factors of 2, 3 and 5. The number is ugly iff what remains is 1.

cards.name: Ugly Number II
cards.trick: Three pointers i2, i3, i5 into the sequence. next = min(u[i2] * 2, u[i3] * 3, u[i5] * 5); advance every pointer that produced next, which also skips duplicates like 6. (Min heap with a set is O(n log n).)

cards.name: Uncommon Words from Two Sentences
cards.trick: Count words across both sentences together. A word is uncommon exactly when its total count is 1.

cards.name: Uncrossed Lines
cards.trick: It is exactly the longest common subsequence of the two arrays. dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 on a match, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Keep only the previous row.

cards.name: Unique Binary Search Trees
cards.trick: The answer is the nth Catalan number: C(i+1) = C(i) * 2 * (2i + 1) / (i + 2). The DP view is dp[n] = sum of dp[root - 1] * dp[n - root] over roots, which is O(n^2) time, O(n) space.

cards.name: Unique Binary Search Trees II
cards.trick: gen(lo, hi) returns all trees on that range: for each root r, combine every tree from gen(lo, r-1) with every tree from gen(r+1, hi). Empty range returns [null]. Memoize by (lo, hi) so subtrees are shared.

cards.name: Unique Email Addresses
cards.trick: Split on '@'. In the local part drop everything after the first '+', then remove all '.'. Add local + '@' + domain to a set and return its size. The domain is untouched.

cards.name: Unique Length-3 Palindromic Subsequences
cards.trick: For each of the 26 letters take its first and last index. The number of distinct letters strictly between them is the count of palindromes with that outer letter. Sum over letters.

cards.name: Unique Paths II
cards.trick: Row-by-row DP in a 1-D array. A cell with an obstacle gets 0, otherwise dp[j] += dp[j - 1] (dp[j] already holds the cell above). Seed dp[0] = 1 unless the start is blocked.

cards.name: Unique Substrings With Equal Digit Frequency
cards.trick: For each start extend right, tracking digit counts, number of distinct digits d and max frequency f. All present digits have equal frequency iff length == d * f. Add a rolling hash (or insert into a trie) of valid substrings to a set to dedupe.

cards.name: Unique Word Abbreviation
cards.time: constructor O(L), isUnique O(k) (L = total chars, k = word length)
cards.trick: Map abbreviation (first + length - 2 + last, words of length <= 2 abbreviate to themselves) to the set of distinct dictionary words with it. A word is unique if its abbreviation is absent or its set is exactly {word}.

cards.name: Unit Conversion II
cards.trick: Conversions form a tree. DFS/BFS from unit 0 gives f[v] = factor from 0 to v (mod 1e9+7). Factor from A to B = f[B] * inverse(f[A]), with the modular inverse by Fermat (pow(x, MOD - 2, MOD)).

cards.name: Valid Palindrome II
cards.trick: Two pointers inward. On the first mismatch, the answer is whether s[l+1..r] or s[l..r-1] is a palindrome (a plain two-pointer check). Only one deletion is allowed, so no more branching.

cards.name: Valid Palindrome III
cards.trick: Min deletions to make a palindrome = n - longest palindromic subsequence (LPS). LPS is the LCS of s and reverse(s), or interval DP. Return true when n - LPS <= k. Roll the DP rows for O(n) space.

cards.name: Valid Perfect Square
cards.trick: Binary search mid in [1, num] comparing mid * mid to num. Return true on exact match. (Newton's method also works; do not use a float sqrt.)

cards.name: Valid Word Abbreviation
cards.trick: Pointer i in word and j in abbr. On letters compare and advance both. On a digit run parse the whole number (reject a leading 0) and skip that many in word. Succeed only if both end exactly.

cards.name: Valid Word Square
cards.trick: For every cell (i, j) of every word check that (j, i) exists, with bounds checks on both indices, and that words[i][j] == words[j][i]. Rows can be ragged.

cards.name: Validate Binary Tree Nodes
cards.trick: Compute indegrees from leftChild and rightChild. Fail if any node has indegree > 1 or there is not exactly one node with indegree 0 (the root). Then DFS/BFS from the root and require that all n nodes get visited.

cards.name: Validate Stack Sequences
cards.trick: Simulate: push each value from pushed, and while the stack top equals popped[j], pop and j++. Valid iff the stack ends empty. (Reusing the pushed array as the stack gives O(1) space.)

cards.name: Verify Preorder Sequence in Binary Search Tree
cards.trick: Monotonic decreasing stack plus a lower bound. For each value, return false if it is below the bound. While the top is smaller than the value, pop and set bound = popped (we moved to a right subtree). Then push. (Using the input array as the stack is O(1) space.)

cards.name: Verifying an Alien Dictionary
cards.trick: Map each char to its rank in order, then compare each adjacent word pair at the first differing char. If one word is a prefix of the other, the shorter must come first, so a longer word before its own prefix is invalid.

cards.name: Walking Robot Simulation
cards.time: O(c + o) (c = commands, o = obstacles; steps per command <= 9)
cards.trick: Put obstacles in a set of coordinate pairs. Simulate one step at a time with a direction index (turns mod 4), stopping at an obstacle, and track the max squared distance at every step.

cards.name: Water Bottles
cards.trick: Each exchange nets numExchange - 1 empties consumed for one more drink, and the last bottle can never be exchanged. Answer = numBottles + (numBottles - 1) // (numExchange - 1). (Looping is O(log n).)

cards.name: Web Crawler
cards.time: O(n * L) (n = urls visited, L = url length)
cards.trick: BFS/DFS from startUrl with a visited set, following only URLs whose hostname equals the start's hostname. Extract the hostname by splitting on '/' (index 2). Return visited.

cards.name: Widest Pair of Indices With Equal Range Sum
cards.trick: Equal range sums means the prefix of (nums1[i] - nums2[i]) is the same at both ends. Store the first index of each prefix value, seeded with {0: -1}, and maximize j - first[prefix].

cards.name: Widest Vertical Area Between Two Points Containing No Points
cards.trick: The y values do not matter. Sort the x-coordinates and return the largest gap between adjacent values.

cards.name: Wiggle Sort
cards.trick: One pass: for i >= 1, if i is odd and nums[i] < nums[i-1], or i is even and nums[i] > nums[i-1], swap them. A swap never breaks the earlier pair. (Sorting then swapping pairs is O(n log n).)

cards.name: Word Abbreviation
cards.time: O(n * L) (n words, L = max length)
cards.trick: Group words by (length, last char). Insert each group into a trie counting passes per node. For each word the prefix length is the first depth where its node count is 1; use it only if the abbreviation is shorter than the word. (Sort with LCP is O(n * L log n).)

cards.name: Word Break II
cards.trick: DFS from index i memoized as i -> all sentences from the suffix, using a word set to test each prefix. Time is bounded by the output size. Run the plain Word Break DP first to return [] fast on impossible inputs.

cards.name: Word Pattern
cards.trick: Split s into words and require the same length as the pattern. Keep two maps, char -> word and word -> char, and fail on any conflict. One map is not enough because the mapping must be a bijection.

cards.name: Word Pattern II
cards.time: O(n^m) worst case (n = len(s), m = len(pattern))
cards.trick: Backtrack over pattern index p and string index i. If the char is already mapped, the next substring must match it. Otherwise try each prefix not already used by another char, map it, recurse, and undo. Keep a set of used substrings.

cards.name: Word Squares
cards.time: O(N * 26^L) worst case (N words of length L)
cards.trick: Backtrack row by row: the next row's required prefix is column k of the rows placed so far. Look up candidates by prefix with a trie or a prefix -> words map. Without the prefix lookup you would scan all words each level.

cards.name: Word Subsets
cards.time: O(A + B) (A = total chars in words1, B = total chars in words2)
cards.trick: A word is universal if it covers every word in words2, so merge words2 into one requirement: for each letter the max count needed across words2. Then check each word in words1 has at least that count of every letter.

cards.name: XOR Queries of a Subarray
cards.trick: Prefix XOR with pre[0] = 0 and pre[i + 1] = pre[i] ^ arr[i]. Query [l, r] = pre[r + 1] ^ pre[l], since equal parts cancel.

cards.name: Zigzag Conversion
cards.trick: Walk the string keeping a row index that flips direction at the top and bottom rows, appending each char to its row's buffer, then join rows. Return s directly when numRows == 1. (Index jumps of 2 * (numRows - 1) avoid buffers.)

cards.name: Zigzag Iterator
cards.space: O(k) (k lists; O(1) for two lists)
cards.trick: Queue of (list, index) pairs. next pops the front, returns its value, and re-enqueues it if elements remain. Generalizes cleanly to k lists. For exactly two lists, two indices and a turn flag also work.

cards.name: Gradient Descent
back: Minimize a differentiable function by repeatedly stepping against its gradient: x_new = x - lr * f'(x).
Pick a start point and learning rate. Each iteration compute the gradient at the current point, subtract lr times the gradient, and repeat for a fixed number of steps or until the gradient is tiny.
Learning rate too large diverges or oscillates, too small crawls. Update all parameters from the same gradient evaluation, and remember it can stall in local minima or flat regions.

cards.name: Sigmoid & ReLU
back: Two activation functions: sigmoid(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) squashes to (0,1), ReLU(x) = max(0, x) zeroes negatives.
Apply each elementwise to the input array. Sigmoid is smooth and used for probabilities; ReLU is cheap and keeps gradients alive for positive inputs.
Naive exp(-x) overflows for large negative x, so use a numerically stable form. Sigmoid saturates (vanishing gradient) and ReLU can die when inputs stay negative.

cards.name: Softmax
back: Turn a vector of scores into a probability distribution: softmax(x_i) = exp(x_i - max(x)) / sum_j exp(x_j - max(x)).
Subtract the max of the vector for stability, exponentiate, then divide by the sum of the exponentials. For batches apply it along the class axis with keepdims so shapes broadcast.
Skipping the max subtraction overflows exp for large logits. Normalizing over the wrong axis is the classic shape bug.

cards.name: Cross-Entropy Loss
back: Loss comparing predicted class probabilities to the true label: L = -sum_i y_i * log(p_i), which for a class index is -log(p[target]).
Take softmax of the logits to get p, pick the probability of the correct class (or dot with the one-hot), take the negative log, and average over the batch.
log(0) gives -inf, so clip with a small eps or use log-softmax on raw logits. Do not apply softmax twice, and be clear whether the reduction is mean or sum.

cards.name: Linear Regression (Forward)
back: Predict a continuous value as a weighted sum of features plus a bias: y_hat = X @ w + b.
With X of shape (n, d) and w of shape (d,), the matrix product gives n predictions; add the scalar bias via broadcasting. Often followed by mean squared error against y.
Shape mismatches such as (n,1) versus (n,) silently broadcast into an (n,n) matrix. Check output shapes explicitly.

cards.name: Linear Regression (Training)
back: Fit linear regression by gradient descent on mean squared error: grad_w = (2/n) X^T (X w + b - y), grad_b = (2/n) sum(X w + b - y).
Initialize w and b, then loop: compute predictions, the error, both gradients, and update w -= lr * grad_w and b -= lr * grad_b for a set number of epochs.
Compute both gradients from the same predictions before updating either parameter. Forgetting the 1/n factor or leaving features unscaled makes the learning rate behave badly.

cards.name: Single Neuron
cards.category: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
back: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
The smallest neural unit: z = w . x + b, then a = activation(z), such as sigmoid.
Compute the dot product of weights and inputs, add the bias, and pass the result through the activation function. This is the forward pass that every larger network repeats.
Do not forget the bias term, and keep the weight and input shapes aligned. Pick an activation whose range matches the target.

cards.name: Backpropagation
cards.category: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
back: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
Compute gradients of the loss with respect to parameters using the chain rule: dL/dw = dL/da * da/dz * dz/dw.
Run the forward pass and cache z and a. Then multiply the loss gradient by the activation derivative and by the input to get dw, and by 1 to get db. Use these in a gradient descent update.
Forgetting the activation derivative term, or recomputing instead of reusing cached forward values, are the usual mistakes. Check signs against the loss definition.

cards.name: Multi-Layer Backpropagation
cards.category: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
back: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
Extend backprop through several layers by propagating an error signal backward: delta_l = (W_{l+1}^T delta_{l+1}) * f'(z_l), dW_l = delta_l a_{l-1}^T.

Store z and a for every layer on the forward pass. Start with delta at the output from the loss, then walk layers in reverse, computing each layer's weight and bias gradients and passing delta back through the transposed weights.
Transposes and batch averaging are where shapes go wrong. Cache every layer's activations, and apply the elementwise activation derivative rather than a matrix product.

cards.name: MLP from Scratch
cards.category: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
back: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
A full multi-layer perceptron built by hand: stacked linear layers with nonlinearities, trained with backprop and gradient descent.
Define layers with weights and biases, implement forward through all layers, compute the loss, run backward to get gradients per layer, then apply the SGD update and repeat over batches.
Zero-initialized weights keep all neurons identical, so use random init. Reset gradients each step and verify shapes layer by layer.

cards.name: Weight Initialization
cards.category: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
back: Machine Learning: Build a Neural Net
Choose initial weights so activations and gradients keep a stable scale across layers: Xavier uses Var(w) = 2 / (fan_in + fan_out), He uses Var(w) = 2 / fan_in.
Sample from a normal or uniform distribution scaled by the formula for the layer's fan_in and fan_out. Use Xavier for tanh or sigmoid and He for ReLU.
Zero or constant init leaves neurons symmetric and stalls learning. Match the scheme to the activation and double check which fan convention the weight shape uses.

cards.name: Pytorch Basics
back: Core PyTorch building blocks: tensors, shape manipulation, matrix ops, and autograd for automatic gradients.
Create tensors, reshape and index them, do math with broadcasting, mark tensors with requires_grad, call backward(), and read .grad.
Gradients accumulate across backward calls until zeroed. view needs contiguous memory, and dtype or device mismatches are common errors.

cards.name: Layer Normalization
back: Normalize each sample across its features: y = gamma * (x - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) + beta.
Compute mean and variance over the last (feature) dimension per example with keepdim, normalize, then scale by learnable gamma and shift by beta.
Normalize over features, not the batch. Use biased variance (unbiased=False), keep eps inside the square root, and mind keepdim so broadcasting works.

cards.name: Batch Normalization
back: Normalize each feature across the batch: y = gamma * (x - batch_mean) / sqrt(batch_var + eps) + beta.
In training compute mean and variance over the batch dimension and update running averages with a momentum. In eval use the stored running mean and variance instead.
Train versus eval behavior is the main trap. Tiny batches give noisy statistics, and the running variance update convention can differ between frameworks.

cards.name: RMS Normalization
back: A simpler norm that rescales by root mean square only: y = gamma * x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps).
Compute mean of squares over the feature dimension, take the square root with eps inside, divide x by it, and multiply by learnable gamma. No mean subtraction and no beta.
Do not center the input like LayerNorm does. Put eps inside the sqrt and reduce over the right axis with keepdim.

cards.name: Training Loop
back: The standard supervised loop: forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer step, repeated over batches and epochs.
For each batch call optimizer.zero_grad(), compute predictions and loss, call loss.backward(), then optimizer.step(). Track loss per epoch and optionally evaluate on held-out data.
Forgetting zero_grad accumulates gradients. Switch model.train() and model.eval() correctly, and wrap evaluation in torch.no_grad().

cards.name: Training Diagnostics
back: Inspect training health through signals like loss curves, gradient norms, and weight statistics to spot exploding or vanishing gradients and overfitting.
Record metrics during training, such as per-layer gradient norms and loss over steps, and compare train versus validation loss. Use them to decide on learning rate, init, or clipping changes.
A single noisy loss reading is not a diagnosis, so look at trends. Compute gradient norms after backward and before the optimizer step.

cards.name: Dead ReLU Detector
back: Find ReLU neurons that output zero for every input, so they receive no gradient and never recover.
Run data through the layer, check which neurons have non-positive pre-activations on all samples, and report the fraction of dead units per layer.
A neuron is dead only if it is inactive across the whole dataset, not just one batch. Common fixes are leaky ReLU, a smaller learning rate, or better init.

cards.name: Digit Classifier
back: Classify 28x28 handwritten digit images into 10 classes with a small neural network, the MNIST-style task.
Flatten each image to 784 values, pass through hidden linear plus ReLU layers to 10 logits, train with cross-entropy and an optimizer over mini-batches, then evaluate accuracy.
Do not apply softmax before nn.CrossEntropyLoss, since it expects raw logits. Normalize pixel values and use eval mode for testing.

cards.name: Word Embeddings
back: Represent each token as a dense learned vector by looking up a row in a vocab_size x dim matrix.
Map tokens to integer ids, index the embedding matrix to get vectors, and compare words with cosine similarity: cos(a,b) = a . b / (|a| |b|).
Handle unknown tokens and padding ids explicitly. Normalize before cosine similarity, and remember embeddings are learned so similarity only means something after training.

cards.name: Intro to Natural Language Processing
back: Introduction to turning text into numbers a model can use: tokenize, build a vocabulary, then map tokens to ids and vectors.
Split text into tokens, assign each an integer id from a vocabulary, and convert sentences to id sequences that feed an embedding layer.
Tokenization choices (case, punctuation, unknown words) change results. Keep train and test preprocessing identical.

cards.name: Sentiment Analysis
back: Classify text as positive or negative by turning tokens into embeddings and predicting a label.
Convert text to token ids, embed them, pool the sequence (for example mean pooling), then apply a linear layer and sigmoid or softmax to get a sentiment probability trained with cross-entropy.
Padding tokens should not count in the pooled average. Use a loss that matches the output (BCEWithLogits for raw logits).

cards.name: Positional Encoding
back: Inject token order into attention using fixed sinusoids: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d)).
Build a (seq_len, d_model) matrix where even columns use sine and odd columns use cosine of position scaled by frequency, then add it to the token embeddings.
Interleave sine and cosine on even and odd indices correctly and add rather than concatenate. Odd d_model needs care with the last column.

cards.name: Self Attention
back: Let each token mix information from others: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.
Project inputs into Q, K, V with linear layers, compute scaled dot-product scores, apply softmax along the key axis, and take the weighted sum of V. A causal mask hides future positions.
Forgetting the 1/sqrt(d_k) scale or softmaxing the wrong axis breaks it. Apply the mask (-inf) before the softmax, not after.

cards.name: Multi Headed Self Attention
back: Run several attention heads in parallel on lower-dimensional slices so each can learn different relations, then recombine them.
Project to Q, K, V, reshape (B,T,d_model) to (B,h,T,d_k) with d_k = d_model / h, attend per head, transpose back, concatenate heads, and apply the output projection W_O.
Reshape and transpose order is the usual bug source, and d_model must divide evenly by the head count. Call contiguous() before view after a transpose.

cards.name: Transformer Block
back: The repeating unit of a transformer: attention for token mixing plus a feed-forward network, each wrapped with normalization and a residual connection.
In pre-LN form: x = x + Attn(LN(x)), then x = x + FFN(LN(x)), where FFN is Linear, GELU or ReLU, Linear with a 4x hidden width. Dropout can follow each sublayer.
Pre-LN versus post-LN placement changes training stability. Residual paths need matching shapes, and decoder blocks need a causal mask.

cards.name: Tokenizer (Byte Pair Encoding)
back: Byte Pair Encoding learns subword units by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols.

Start from characters or bytes, count adjacent pair frequencies, merge the top pair into a new token, and repeat for a set number of merges. To encode, apply the learned merges in the order they were learned.
Define deterministic tie-breaking, count overlapping pairs correctly (for example in aaa), and apply merges in learned order at encode time.

cards.name: Build Vocabulary
back: Create the token-to-id mapping (and its inverse) a model uses to read and write text.
Collect the unique tokens from the corpus, add special tokens such as padding and unknown, assign ids in a deterministic order, and expose encode and decode lookups.
Sort or otherwise fix the ordering so ids are reproducible. Always have an unknown-token fallback for unseen input.

cards.name: Tokenization Edge Cases
back: Make a tokenizer robust to awkward input such as empty strings, unknown characters, repeated whitespace, and multi-byte unicode.
Check behavior on each tricky input, ensure encode then decode round-trips, and handle unknown or special tokens through defined fallbacks.
Characters can span multiple bytes, so byte-level and character-level handling differ. Verify round-trip equality rather than assuming it.

cards.name: GPT Data Loader
back: Produce training batches for next-token prediction by sampling fixed-length windows from a token stream.
Pick random start indices, take x = tokens[i : i+T] and y = tokens[i+1 : i+T+1], stack batch_size of them into tensors, and return (x, y).
Targets are inputs shifted by one token, and the start index must stay at most len(tokens) - T - 1 to avoid running off the end.

cards.name: GPT Dataset
back: Wrap a tokenized corpus as a dataset whose items are (input, target) windows for next-token prediction.
Implement __len__ and __getitem__ so index i returns tokens[i:i+T] as input and tokens[i+1:i+T+1] as target, usable with a DataLoader.
Dataset length must account for the block size so the last target stays in range. Targets are shifted one step, not the same slice.

cards.name: Code GPT
back: Assemble a decoder-only GPT: embeddings, stacked causal transformer blocks, and a language-model head.
Sum token and positional embeddings, pass through N transformer blocks with a causal mask, apply a final LayerNorm, then a linear head to vocab size to produce logits of shape (B, T, V).
Without the causal mask the model sees future tokens and cheats. Keep positions within block_size and match shapes between blocks.

cards.name: Train Your GPT
back: Train the GPT to predict the next token using cross-entropy over every position.
Get batches (x, y), run the model for logits, flatten to (B*T, V) and targets to (B*T), compute cross-entropy, backprop, and step an optimizer such as AdamW. Monitor loss over iterations.
Flatten logits and targets consistently or the loss shape is wrong. Gradient clipping and a learning rate warmup help stability, and zero grads each step.

cards.name: Make GPT Talk Back
back: Generate text autoregressively by sampling one token at a time from the trained model.
Start from a prompt, crop the context to block_size, run the model, take the last position's logits, divide by temperature, softmax, sample a token, append it, and repeat.
Only the last position's logits predict the next token. Crop the context so it never exceeds block_size, and run in eval mode under no_grad.

cards.name: KV-Cache
back: Speed up autoregressive decoding by caching each layer's past keys and values instead of recomputing them every step.
On each new token compute only its Q, K, V, append K and V to the cache, and attend the new query over all cached keys and values. Prefill handles the prompt in one pass.
Cache memory grows linearly with sequence length. Position indices must continue from the cached length, and the cache is for inference, not training.

cards.name: Grouped Query Attention
back: Attention variant where many query heads share a smaller number of key and value heads, cutting KV memory.
Use n_q query heads and n_kv key/value heads with n_q divisible by n_kv. Repeat each KV head across its group of query heads, then run standard scaled dot-product attention.
Head grouping order matters (repeat_interleave versus repeat). n_kv = 1 gives multi-query attention and n_kv = n_q gives standard multi-head attention.

cards.name: Factory Method Pattern
back: Creational pattern: define an interface for creating objects and let a factory or subclass decide which concrete class to instantiate.
Callers ask a factory method (for example create(kind)) for a Product. The factory returns a concrete implementation of a shared Product interface, so client code depends only on the abstraction.

Use it when the concrete type varies at runtime. Skip it for a single concrete class, since extra indirection is overkill. A growing if/else in the factory violates open-closed unless you use a registry.

cards.name: Singleton Pattern
back: Creational pattern: guarantee a class has exactly one instance and provide a global access point to it.
Make the constructor private, hold the instance in a static field, and expose getInstance() that creates it lazily on first use and returns the same object afterward.

Not thread-safe by default, so guard creation with a lock or double-checked locking. It is global state that hurts testability; prefer dependency injection unless one shared instance is truly required.

cards.name: Builder Pattern
back: Creational pattern: construct a complex object step by step, separating construction from the final representation.
A Builder exposes chained setter steps (setX, setY) and a build() method that validates and returns the finished immutable object. An optional Director fixes common step sequences.
Best when there are many optional parameters, replacing telescoping constructors. Validate required fields in build(), and avoid it for simple objects with a few fields.

cards.name: Prototype Pattern
back: Creational pattern: create new objects by cloning an existing instance instead of building from scratch.
Objects implement a clone() method that returns a copy. Clients keep prototypes (often in a registry) and copy them, then tweak the copy.
Shallow versus deep copy is the classic trap: shared mutable references leak between clones. Use it when construction is expensive or the concrete class is unknown.

cards.name: Adapter Pattern
back: Structural pattern: convert one interface into another that clients expect so incompatible classes can work together.
The Adapter implements the target interface and wraps an Adaptee, translating each call (and data format) to the Adaptee's methods.
Use it to integrate legacy or third-party code you cannot change. It differs from Decorator (which keeps the same interface) and Facade (which simplifies many interfaces).

cards.name: Decorator Pattern
back: Structural pattern: attach extra behavior to an object dynamically by wrapping it, without changing its class.
Decorators implement the same Component interface and hold a wrapped Component. Each adds behavior before or after delegating, and they can be stacked in any order.
Wrapping order can change results, and many small wrapper classes complicate debugging. Prefer it over subclass explosion when features combine freely.

cards.name: Facade Pattern
back: Structural pattern: provide one simple interface to a complex subsystem of many classes.
A Facade class exposes a few high-level methods and internally coordinates the subsystem objects in the right order. Clients call the facade instead of each component.
It simplifies but does not forbid direct subsystem access. A facade that accumulates logic becomes a god object, so keep it a thin coordinator.

cards.name: Strategy Pattern
back: Behavioral pattern: define a family of interchangeable algorithms and let the client choose which one to use at runtime.
A Strategy interface declares the algorithm method. Concrete strategies implement it, and a Context holds a strategy reference and delegates to it, allowing swaps without changing the context.
It replaces large if/else or switch blocks on behavior. Clients must know the strategies, and trivial cases may not justify the extra classes.

cards.name: Observer Pattern
back: Behavioral pattern: when a subject changes state, all subscribed observers are notified and updated automatically.
The Subject keeps a list of Observers with attach, detach and notify methods. Observers implement update(), and the subject calls it on each one when its state changes.
Forgetting to unsubscribe causes memory leaks, and notification order is unspecified. Watch for update cascades and avoid modifying the observer list during notification.

cards.name: State Pattern
back: Behavioral pattern: let an object change its behavior when its internal state changes, as if it switched class.
A Context holds a current State object and delegates requests to it. Each concrete State implements behavior for that state and may set the context's next state to drive transitions.
It replaces big state-based conditionals, but adds many classes. Define valid transitions clearly, and for a very small state machine a simple enum may be enough.

cards.name: Build System
back: A phased AI-assisted coding problem on a Python DependencyGraph that manages tasks and their dependencies for a build system.

Phase 1 is bug fixing: the reverse adjacency map is keyed by the dependency instead of the task, and the in-degree update in topological_order is applied to the wrong node. Later phases extend the graph code.
Topological ordering bugs come from mixing up edge direction. Read the existing code and tests before changing anything, and check later phase requirements on the page.

cards.name: Delivery Grid
back: A phased AI-assisted coding problem on a Python Grid class modeling a city for a delivery robot, with blocked cells, traffic costs, pickup and depot cells, and teleport pads.
Phase 1 fixes three bugs in neighbor bounds, move cost, and stale teleport state. Later phases extend the grid logic, building on the same Grid class.
Bounds checks, cost paid on entry, and state that is not reset are classic grid pitfalls. Confirm later phase details on the page.

cards.name: Streaming Analytics
back: A three-phase AI-assisted coding problem on a time-based SlidingWindow that aggregates timestamped events (count, sum, average, min, max, percentile).
Phase 1 fixes two bugs in _evict (an off-by-one eviction boundary and stale min/max after eviction). Phase 2 implements the solution and phase 3 optimizes it.
Window boundary inclusivity and keeping min/max correct after eviction are the pitfalls. Optimization usually means avoiding rescans of the whole window.

cards.name: Triplet Draw
back: A three-phase AI-assisted coding problem on a playing-card codebase: fix bugs, implement features, then optimize.
Phase 1 fixes three bugs: card equality ignores suit, aces ignore the ace_high setting, and face cards score as their rank instead of 10. Later phases build on the card and hand logic.
Equality and scoring rules need to match the stated spec exactly. Confirm later phase requirements on the page.

cards.name: Word Bag Max
back: A three-phase AI-assisted coding problem: select words whose letter sets do not overlap so the bag covers the most unique letters.
Phase 1 fixes three bugs in the provided CharSet and WordBag code, phase 2 implements the solution, and phase 3 optimizes it. Overlap checks on letter sets drive the search.
The selection is a combinatorial search, so naive approaches blow up and optimization matters. Check the exact scoring rules on the page.

cards.name: Word Reveal
back: A three-phase AI-assisted coding problem: a Hangman-style, case-insensitive game where players guess letters to reveal a hidden word.
Phase 1 fixes three bugs: case-sensitive input validation, case-sensitive secret matching, and an inverted completion check. Phase 2 implements features and phase 3 optimizes.
Normalize case consistently for both guesses and the secret word, and double check boolean conditions such as completion. Confirm later phase details on the page.

cards.name: Customers With Positive Revenue
back: Plain row filter on two conditions. No join or aggregation is needed.
SELECT customer_id FROM Customers WHERE year = 2021 AND revenue > 0
revenue can be NULL, and NULL > 0 is not true, so those rows drop out (usually what you want). The year is fixed at 2021 in the original problem.

cards.name: Customers Without Orders
back: Anti-join: LEFT JOIN the child table and keep rows where the child key IS NULL.
SELECT c.name AS Customers FROM Customers c LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.customerId = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
Test IS NULL on the right table's primary key, not on a column that could legitimately be NULL. NOT IN also works but breaks if the subquery returns any NULL.

cards.name: Calculate Special Bonus
back: Conditional value per row with CASE or IF. No grouping.
SELECT employee_id, IF(employee_id % 2 = 1 AND name NOT LIKE 'M%', salary, 0) AS bonus FROM Employees ORDER BY employee_id
Bonus applies only when the id is odd AND the name does not start with M; otherwise it is 0, not NULL. Remember the ORDER BY employee_id.

cards.name: Customers Who Bought A and B but Not C
back: Group by customer and use conditional aggregation in HAVING to assert present A, present B, absent C.

SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name HAVING SUM(o.product_name = 'A') > 0 AND SUM(o.product_name = 'B') > 0 AND SUM(o.product_name = 'C') = 0 ORDER BY c.customer_id
Filtering rows with WHERE product_name = 'A' cannot express 'not C'; the logic has to live in HAVING over the whole group. Inner join drops customers with no orders, which is correct here.

cards.name: Highest Grade For Each Student
back: Window ROW_NUMBER over each student ordered by grade descending, then course_id ascending as the tie breaker.
SELECT student_id, course_id, grade FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY student_id ORDER BY grade DESC, course_id ASC) AS rn FROM Enrollments) t WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY student_id
Ties on the top grade must resolve to the smallest course_id, so use ROW_NUMBER with the tie breaker, not RANK (which would return several rows).

cards.name: Combine Two Tables
back: LEFT JOIN from the table whose rows must all appear.
SELECT p.firstName, p.lastName, a.city, a.state FROM Person p LEFT JOIN Address a ON a.personId = p.personId
Using INNER JOIN would silently drop people with no address. Put Person on the left.

cards.name: Sellers With No Sales
back: Anti-join: sellers that do not appear in orders for the target year.
SELECT seller_name FROM Seller WHERE seller_id NOT IN (SELECT seller_id FROM Orders WHERE YEAR(sale_date) = 2020) ORDER BY seller_name
The year filter belongs inside the subquery, not outside. If the subquery column can be NULL, NOT IN returns nothing; use NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN IS NULL to be safe.

cards.name: Top Travellers
back: LEFT JOIN users to rides, SUM distance per user, and COALESCE missing sums to 0.
SELECT u.name, IFNULL(SUM(r.distance), 0) AS travelled_distance FROM Users u LEFT JOIN Rides r ON r.user_id = u.id GROUP BY u.id, u.name ORDER BY travelled_distance DESC, u.name ASC
Group by u.id, not name alone, because names can repeat. Users with no rides need LEFT JOIN plus IFNULL, and the sort has a name tie breaker.

cards.name: Sales Person
back: Exclude salespeople who have any order tied to company RED; a NOT IN or NOT EXISTS anti-join.
SELECT name FROM SalesPerson WHERE sales_id NOT IN (SELECT o.sales_id FROM Orders o JOIN Company c ON c.com_id = o.com_id WHERE c.name = 'RED')
Salespeople with no orders at all must still be returned, so do not start from Orders. Beware NULL in the NOT IN subquery.

cards.name: Evaluate Boolean Expression
back: Join the Variables table twice (left and right operand) and pick the comparison with CASE on the operator.

SELECT e.left_operand, e.operator, e.right_operand, IF(CASE e.operator WHEN '>' THEN v1.value > v2.value WHEN '<' THEN v1.value < v2.value ELSE v1.value = v2.value END, 'true', 'false') AS value FROM Expressions e JOIN Variables v1 ON v1.name = e.left_operand JOIN Variables v2 ON v2.name = e.right_operand
The output column is the strings 'true' or 'false', not 1 or 0, so wrap the comparison in IF. Two separate aliases of Variables are required.

cards.name: Team Scores in Football Tournament
back: LEFT JOIN teams to matches where the team is host or guest, then SUM points with CASE: 3 for win, 1 for draw, 0 for loss.

SELECT t.team_id, t.team_name, IFNULL(SUM(CASE WHEN m.host_team = t.team_id THEN (CASE WHEN m.host_goals > m.guest_goals THEN 3 WHEN m.host_goals = m.guest_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ELSE (CASE WHEN m.guest_goals > m.host_goals THEN 3 WHEN m.host_goals = m.guest_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) END), 0) AS num_points FROM Teams t LEFT JOIN Matches m ON t.team_id IN (m.host_team, m.guest_team) GROUP BY t.team_id, t.team_name ORDER BY num_points DESC, t.team_id ASC
Teams with zero matches still need a row with 0 points, so LEFT JOIN plus IFNULL. Score the same team from both host and guest perspectives.

cards.name: The Latest Login in 2020
back: Filter to the 2020 window, then MAX(time_stamp) per user.
SELECT user_id, MAX(time_stamp) AS last_stamp FROM Logins WHERE time_stamp >= '2020-01-01' AND time_stamp < '2021-01-01' GROUP BY user_id
Use a half-open range; BETWEEN with '2020-12-31' would miss logins later that day on a datetime column. Users with no 2020 login are not returned.

cards.name: Game Play Analysis I
back: Simple GROUP BY with MIN to get the first date per player.
SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_login FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id
Nothing tricky; the output column alias must be first_login. Do not join or window for this one.

cards.name: Warehouse Manager
back: Join stock to product dimensions and SUM units * width * length * height per warehouse.
SELECT w.name AS warehouse_name, SUM(w.units * p.Width * p.Length * p.Height) AS volume FROM Warehouse w JOIN Products p ON p.product_id = w.product_id GROUP BY w.name
The warehouse name repeats across product rows, so group by name. Multiply units by the product volume before summing, not after.

cards.name: Customer Placing the Largest Number of Orders
back: GROUP BY customer, ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, take the top row.
SELECT customer_number FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_number ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1
LIMIT 1 only works because the problem guarantees a single winner. For ties, compare COUNT(*) to the maximum in a subquery or use RANK().

cards.name: Find Total Time Spent by Each Employee
back: Subtract out_time minus in_time per row, then SUM per day and employee.
SELECT event_day AS day, emp_id, SUM(out_time - in_time) AS total_time FROM Employees GROUP BY event_day, emp_id
An employee can have several in/out rows per day, so the SUM is needed. Group by both day and emp_id.

cards.name: Immediate Food Delivery I
back: Average of a boolean expression gives the proportion; multiply by 100 and round.
SELECT ROUND(100 * AVG(order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date), 2) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery
Round to 2 decimals as required. The comparison yields 1 or 0 in MySQL, which is why AVG works; use SUM(CASE ...)/COUNT(*) on other databases.

cards.name: Apples & Oranges
back: Conditional SUM per date: apples count positive, oranges negative.
SELECT sale_date, SUM(IF(fruit = 'apples', sold_num, -sold_num)) AS diff FROM Sales GROUP BY sale_date ORDER BY sale_date
The difference is apples minus oranges, in that order. Each date has exactly one row per fruit, so no extra handling for missing fruit.

cards.name: Number of Calls Between Two Persons
back: Normalize each pair with LEAST and GREATEST so (a,b) and (b,a) collapse into one group.
SELECT LEAST(from_id, to_id) AS person1, GREATEST(from_id, to_id) AS person2, COUNT(*) AS call_count, SUM(duration) AS total_duration FROM Calls GROUP BY person1, person2
Without the normalization you get two groups per pair. Group by the normalized expressions, not the raw columns.

cards.name: Bank Account Summary II
back: Join users to transactions, SUM per account, filter with HAVING.
SELECT u.name, SUM(t.amount) AS balance FROM Users u JOIN Transactions t ON t.account = u.account GROUP BY u.account, u.name HAVING SUM(t.amount) > 10000
Strictly greater than 10000. The filter on the aggregate goes in HAVING, not WHERE.

cards.name: Duplicate Emails
back: GROUP BY the column and keep groups with COUNT greater than 1.
SELECT email FROM Person GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
Use HAVING, not WHERE, since it filters on an aggregate. NULL emails form their own group, so exclude them if they exist.

cards.name: Actors and Directors Who Cooperated At Least Three Times
back: GROUP BY the actor-director pair and require at least 3 rows.
SELECT actor_id, director_id FROM ActorDirector GROUP BY actor_id, director_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
At least three means >= 3. Group by both columns together, not each separately.

cards.name: Customer Order Frequency
back: Join orders to product prices, then conditional SUM of quantity * price for June and July in HAVING.

SELECT c.customer_id, c.name FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = o.product_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name HAVING SUM(IF(o.order_date >= '2020-06-01' AND o.order_date < '2020-07-01', o.quantity * p.price, 0)) >= 100 AND SUM(IF(o.order_date >= '2020-07-01' AND o.order_date < '2020-08-01', o.quantity * p.price, 0)) >= 100
Both months must independently reach 100, so two separate conditional sums joined by AND. Use half-open date ranges to avoid end-of-month time problems.

cards.name: Daily Leads and Partners
back: GROUP BY date and make with COUNT(DISTINCT) for leads and partners.
SELECT date_id, make_name, COUNT(DISTINCT lead_id) AS unique_leads, COUNT(DISTINCT partner_id) AS unique_partners FROM DailySales GROUP BY date_id, make_name
Plain COUNT(*) would count duplicate rows. Use DISTINCT inside each COUNT separately.

cards.name: Friendly Movies Streamed Last Month
back: Join the program schedule to content and filter on kid-friendly flag, movie type, and the June 2020 date range.

SELECT DISTINCT c.title FROM Content c JOIN TVProgram t ON t.content_id = c.content_id WHERE c.Kids_content = 'Y' AND c.content_type = 'Movies' AND t.program_date >= '2020-06-01' AND t.program_date < '2020-07-01'
