A movie can air many times in the month, so DISTINCT is needed. Use a half-open date range because program_date may carry a time part.

cards.name: Countries You Can Safely Invest In
back: Extract the country code from the phone prefix, count each call for both caller and callee with UNION ALL, then compare each country's average duration to the global average.

WITH c AS (SELECT caller_id AS id, duration FROM Calls UNION ALL SELECT callee_id, duration FROM Calls) SELECT co.name AS country FROM c JOIN Person p ON p.id = c.id JOIN Country co ON co.country_code = LEFT(p.phone_number, 3) GROUP BY co.name HAVING AVG(c.duration) > (SELECT AVG(duration) FROM c)
Use UNION ALL, not UNION, or identical calls collapse and averages change. The comparison is strictly greater than the global average over all call legs.

cards.name: Consecutive Available Seats
back: Self join the seat table on adjacent ids where both seats are free.
SELECT DISTINCT a.seat_id FROM Cinema a JOIN Cinema b ON ABS(a.seat_id - b.seat_id) = 1 AND a.free = 1 AND b.free = 1 ORDER BY a.seat_id
DISTINCT is required since a seat in the middle of a run matches two neighbors. Alternative: LAG and LEAD window functions.

cards.name: Rearrange Products Table
back: Unpivot columns into rows with one SELECT per column glued by UNION ALL.

SELECT product_id, 'store1' AS store, store1 AS price FROM Products WHERE store1 IS NOT NULL UNION ALL SELECT product_id, 'store2', store2 FROM Products WHERE store2 IS NOT NULL UNION ALL SELECT product_id, 'store3', store3 FROM Products WHERE store3 IS NOT NULL
NULL prices mean the product is not sold at that store, so filter them out in each branch. UNION ALL avoids the needless dedup of plain UNION.

cards.name: Shortest Distance in a Line
back: Self join all distinct pairs and take the minimum absolute difference, or use LAG over sorted x.
SELECT MIN(ABS(a.x - b.x)) AS shortest FROM Point a JOIN Point b ON a.x <> b.x
Exclude the pair of a point with itself (distance 0). The self join is quadratic; for large tables, ORDER BY x with LAG(x) and MIN of the gap is O(n log n).

cards.name: Employees With Missing Information
back: Find ids present in one table but not the other (two anti-joins) and combine them with UNION.

SELECT employee_id FROM Employees WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Salaries) UNION SELECT employee_id FROM Salaries WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Employees) ORDER BY employee_id
MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN, hence the two-sided anti-join. Use UNION so an id cannot appear twice, and sort the result.

cards.name: Page Recommendations
back: Collect user 1's friends from both columns of the friendship table, then pick pages those friends like that user 1 does not.

SELECT DISTINCT page_id AS recommended_page FROM Likes WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user2_id FROM Friendship WHERE user1_id = 1 UNION SELECT user1_id FROM Friendship WHERE user2_id = 1) AND page_id NOT IN (SELECT page_id FROM Likes WHERE user_id = 1)
Friendship is stored in one direction, so check both columns. Use DISTINCT since several friends may like the same page.

cards.name: Tree Node
back: Classify each node with CASE: Root if parent is NULL, Inner if it is some node's parent, otherwise Leaf.
SELECT id, CASE WHEN p_id IS NULL THEN 'Root' WHEN id IN (SELECT p_id FROM Tree WHERE p_id IS NOT NULL) THEN 'Inner' ELSE 'Leaf' END AS type FROM Tree
Check Root first. The subquery must exclude NULL p_id values or IN/NOT IN logic breaks. A single-node tree is Root, not Leaf.

cards.name: Game Play Analysis III
back: Running total with SUM() OVER partitioned by player and ordered by date.
SELECT player_id, event_date, SUM(games_played) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_date) AS games_played_so_far FROM Activity
The ORDER BY inside OVER makes the sum cumulative. Rows with the same event_date for one player would be treated as peers, but the key (player_id, event_date) is unique here.

cards.name: Grand Slam Titles
back: Join players to any championship year they won in any of the four tournament columns, then count the matching columns per row.

SELECT p.player_id, p.player_name, SUM((c.Wimbledon = p.player_id) + (c.Fr_open = p.player_id) + (c.US_open = p.player_id) + (c.Au_open = p.player_id)) AS grand_slams_count FROM Players p JOIN Championships c ON p.player_id IN (c.Wimbledon, c.Fr_open, c.US_open, c.Au_open) GROUP BY p.player_id, p.player_name
Players with zero titles must not appear, so INNER JOIN is intended. A player can win several slams in the same year, hence summing the four boolean terms.

cards.name: Neetflex Banned Accounts
back: Likely a join or anti-join between an accounts table and a banned or status table to flag restricted accounts.
SELECT a.account_id FROM Accounts a JOIN Banned b ON b.account_id = a.account_id
The exact schema and conditions for this NeetCode-original problem are not known, so this is a generic shape. Check the problem statement for the real tables and any date or status filters.

cards.name: Students With Invalid Departments
back: Anti-join: students whose department_id has no match in the Departments table.
SELECT s.id, s.name FROM Students s LEFT JOIN Departments d ON d.id = s.department_id WHERE d.id IS NULL
Test IS NULL on d.id, the key of the joined table. NOT IN works too but fails if Departments.id could be NULL.

cards.name: Find the Team Size
back: Window COUNT partitioned by team so every employee row carries its team's size.
SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id) AS team_size FROM Employee
A window function keeps all employee rows; a plain GROUP BY would collapse them. A join to a grouped subquery is the equivalent without windows.

cards.name: Game Play Analysis II
back: Find each player's first login date, then return the device used on that date.
SELECT player_id, device_id FROM Activity WHERE (player_id, event_date) IN (SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id)
Do not just SELECT device_id with MIN(event_date) in a GROUP BY; the device would be arbitrary. Match on the (player, first date) pair or use ROW_NUMBER.

cards.name: Department Highest Salary
back: Match each employee to their department's maximum salary, computed per department in a subquery.

SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM Employee e JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.departmentId WHERE (e.departmentId, e.salary) IN (SELECT departmentId, MAX(salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY departmentId)
Ties for the top salary must all be returned, which the pair match handles. RANK() over (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1 is the window alternative.

cards.name: The Most Recent Orders for Each Product
back: Keep the order rows whose date equals each product's latest order date (ties included), then join product names.

SELECT p.product_name, o.product_id, o.order_id, o.order_date FROM Orders o JOIN Products p ON p.product_id = o.product_id WHERE (o.product_id, o.order_date) IN (SELECT product_id, MAX(order_date) FROM Orders GROUP BY product_id) ORDER BY p.product_name, o.product_id, o.order_id
Several orders can share the latest date, so return all of them (RANK = 1, not ROW_NUMBER). Follow the required three-column sort order.

cards.name: The Most Recent Three Orders
back: ROW_NUMBER per customer ordered by date descending, keep rn <= 3.

SELECT customer_name, customer_id, order_id, order_date FROM (SELECT c.name AS customer_name, o.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_date DESC) AS rn FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id) t WHERE rn <= 3 ORDER BY customer_name, customer_id, order_date DESC
Window functions cannot be filtered in the same SELECT, so wrap in a subquery. Customers with fewer than 3 orders just return what they have.

cards.name: Maximum Transaction Each Day
back: RANK transactions by amount within each calendar day and keep rank 1 so ties are all returned.
SELECT transaction_id FROM (SELECT transaction_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY DATE(day) ORDER BY amount DESC) AS r FROM Transactions) t WHERE r = 1 ORDER BY transaction_id
Partition by the date part if day is a datetime. Use RANK, not ROW_NUMBER, to keep ties.

cards.name: Project Employees III
back: Join employees to projects, RANK by experience_years within each project, keep rank 1.

SELECT project_id, employee_id FROM (SELECT p.project_id, p.employee_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.project_id ORDER BY e.experience_years DESC) AS r FROM Project p JOIN Employee e ON e.employee_id = p.employee_id) t WHERE r = 1
Ties on experience must all be returned, so RANK not ROW_NUMBER.

cards.name: Find the Start and End Number of Continuous Ranges
back: Gaps and islands: subtract ROW_NUMBER from the value; consecutive numbers share the same difference, so group on it.
SELECT MIN(log_id) AS start_id, MAX(log_id) AS end_id FROM (SELECT log_id, log_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY log_id) AS grp FROM Logs) t GROUP BY grp ORDER BY start_id
The trick relies on unique, sorted ids; duplicates would break the constant difference. A gap changes grp and starts a new island.

cards.name: The Most Frequently Ordered Products for Each Customer
back: Count orders per customer-product pair, RANK by count within each customer, keep rank 1 for ties.

WITH t AS (SELECT customer_id, product_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS r FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id, product_id) SELECT t.customer_id, t.product_id, p.product_name FROM t JOIN Products p ON p.product_id = t.product_id WHERE t.r = 1
A window over an aggregate is allowed because the window runs after GROUP BY. Return every tied product, and only customers who ordered something.

cards.name: Biggest Window Between Visits
back: LEAD gives each visit's next visit date, with 2021-01-01 as the default for the last one; the max DATEDIFF per user is the answer.

SELECT user_id, MAX(DATEDIFF(nxt, visit_date)) AS biggest_window FROM (SELECT user_id, visit_date, LEAD(visit_date, 1, '2021-01-01') OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS nxt FROM UserVisits) t GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id
Do not forget the final gap from the last visit to the 2021-01-01 reference date. The LEAD default argument handles it.

cards.name: All People Report to the Given Manager
back: Walk the reporting chain up to 3 levels, from manager 1 downward, using a recursive CTE with a depth limit.

WITH RECURSIVE r AS (SELECT employee_id, 1 AS d FROM Employees WHERE manager_id = 1 AND employee_id <> 1 UNION ALL SELECT e.employee_id, r.d + 1 FROM Employees e JOIN r ON e.manager_id = r.employee_id WHERE r.d < 3) SELECT employee_id FROM r
Employee 1 usually has manager_id = 1 (reports to self), so exclude them or the recursion loops. Equivalent non-recursive answer: three self joins.

cards.name: Find the Quiet Students in All Exams
back: Compute each exam's max and min with window functions; a quiet student never scored either extreme in any exam they took.

SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name FROM Student s JOIN (SELECT student_id, score, MAX(score) OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id) AS mx, MIN(score) OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id) AS mn FROM Exam) e ON e.student_id = s.student_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name HAVING SUM(e.score = e.mx OR e.score = e.mn) = 0 ORDER BY s.student_id
Students who took no exam must be excluded; the inner join does that. Compare to the max and min of that exam, not the global ones.

cards.name: Find the Subtasks That Did Not Execute
back: Generate every subtask id 1..N per task with a recursive CTE, then anti-join against the Executed table.

WITH RECURSIVE s AS (SELECT task_id, subtasks_count AS n FROM Tasks UNION ALL SELECT task_id, n - 1 FROM s WHERE n > 1) SELECT s.task_id, s.n AS subtask_id FROM s LEFT JOIN Executed e ON e.task_id = s.task_id AND e.subtask_id = s.n WHERE e.task_id IS NULL
The task_id and subtask_id must both be in the join condition. Counting down avoids needing a numbers table.

cards.name: Report Contiguous Dates
back: Union failed and succeeded dates with a state label, then gaps and islands: date minus ROW_NUMBER per state is constant within a run.

SELECT state AS period_state, MIN(d) AS start_date, MAX(d) AS end_date FROM (SELECT state, d, DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY d) DAY) AS g FROM (SELECT 'failed' AS state, fail_date AS d FROM Failed WHERE fail_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' UNION ALL SELECT 'succeeded', success_date FROM Succeeded WHERE success_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31') a) b GROUP BY state, g ORDER BY start_date
Restrict to 2019 before computing islands. Partition by state so failed and succeeded runs are numbered independently; sort the output by start_date.

cards.name: Design LeetCode
back: Asynchronous judging: submissions go onto a queue and are run by an autoscaled pool of sandboxed workers. Contest leaderboards use a Redis sorted set.

Client POSTs code to an API service that saves the submission and enqueues a job (Kafka or SQS). Workers pull jobs, run the code in isolated containers or gVisor/Firecracker sandboxes with CPU, memory, and time limits against the stored test cases, then write a verdict to the DB. The client polls or gets a websocket push. Problems and test data live in SQL plus object storage; the leaderboard is a Redis ZSET.

Untrusted code is the top risk: strict sandboxing, no network, resource limits. Contests cause bursts, so queue depth and worker autoscaling matter, and per-language images and consistent timing need care.

cards.name: Design URL Shortener
back: Generate a unique short key (base62 of a counter, or pre-generated key range) and serve reads from a cache-heavy key-value store. Choice of 301 vs 302 redirect.

POST /urls takes a long URL and returns a short code; GET /{code} redirects. Codes come from a key generation service (counter ranges per app server, or base62 of a Snowflake ID) so there are no collisions. Mapping is stored in a KV store like DynamoDB or Cassandra keyed by code, with Redis or CDN caching for hot links. Click analytics are sent asynchronously through a queue.

Read to write is very high, so cache and replicas matter. Probes: collision handling, 7 chars of base62 gives about 3.5 trillion codes, custom aliases, expiry, 301 (cacheable, loses analytics) vs 302, and hot-key abuse.

cards.name: Design Webhook
back: Reliable at-least-once event delivery to customer HTTP endpoints, using a durable queue, retries with exponential backoff, and signed payloads.

Event producers publish to a queue (Kafka). A dispatcher looks up each subscriber's endpoint and secret, then workers POST the payload with a short timeout and an HMAC signature header. Failures go to retry queues with exponential backoff and jitter, and eventually a dead letter queue. Every attempt is logged in a delivery store so customers can inspect and replay events.

One slow or dead endpoint can block others, so isolate per endpoint or tenant, rate limit, and use circuit breakers. Probes: ordering vs at-least-once, idempotency keys, secret rotation, SSRF protection, and replay.

cards.name: Design Google Docs
back: Real-time collaborative editing using Operational Transform or CRDTs, with all edits to a document routed through one collaboration server.

Clients hold a websocket to a collaboration server chosen by document ID. Each edit is sent as an operation; the server transforms it against concurrent ops (OT), assigns a total order, appends it to a persisted operation log, and broadcasts to other clients. Periodic snapshots allow fast loading. Separate services handle presence and cursors, permissions, and version history.

Probes: OT (central server, simpler state) vs CRDT (decentralized, metadata growth), offline editing and reconnect, log compaction, hot documents with many editors, and permission checks on every operation.

cards.name: Design Spotify Top K Songs
back: Stream aggregation of play counts with windowed counters, and a mergeable top-K structure (heap or count-min sketch plus heap).

Play events go into Kafka partitioned by song ID. Stream processors (Flink or Spark Streaming) count plays per tumbling or sliding window and keep a local top K per partition. A merger combines partition tops into the global top K and writes it to Redis or a serving DB. API reads are served from the cache. Batch jobs recompute exact long-range windows (day, week).
Trade-off: exact counts vs approximate (count-min sketch) to save memory. Probes: hot song skew, late events and watermarks, window semantics, and merge correctness when keys are partitioned.

cards.name: Design Yelp
back: Proximity search over a geospatial index (geohash, quadtree, or S2) combined with ranking; very read-heavy.

A business service owns CRUD in a relational DB; changes are streamed into a search index (Elasticsearch or a geohash-keyed store). A query converts lat/lon and radius into covering geohash cells (plus neighbors), filters by category, and ranks by distance, rating, and relevance. Reviews are a separate service with ratings aggregated asynchronously; photos live in object storage behind a CDN.
Probes: geohash boundary problem (query neighbor cells), uneven density (quadtree or adaptive cells), eventual consistency of ratings, caching popular areas, and review abuse.

cards.name: Design Rate Limiter
back: Token bucket or sliding window counters kept in a shared fast store (Redis) and enforced at the gateway.

A middleware at the API gateway builds a key from user, IP, or API key plus the rule, and runs an atomic Redis Lua script that refills and decrements the token bucket. If no tokens remain it returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. Rules come from a config service and are cached locally; Redis is sharded by key for scale.

Probes: algorithm trade-offs (fixed window bursts at boundaries, sliding window log memory, token bucket allows bursts), atomicity and race conditions, fail-open vs fail-closed when Redis is down, and multi-region consistency.

cards.name: Design Pastebin
back: Split small metadata from large paste content: metadata in a DB, content in object storage, keys from a pre-generated key service.

POST /pastes takes content, expiry, and visibility; a key service hands out a unique key. Content is stored in S3 and metadata (key, path, owner, expiry) in a KV or SQL DB. GET /{key} checks Redis or CDN, then the DB, then S3. A cleanup job removes expired pastes.
Probes: read-heavy skew and caching, paste size limits, expiry via TTL vs lazy deletion, spam and abuse, and key collisions. It is the URL shortener design plus blob storage.

cards.name: Design Realtime Monitoring System
back: Metrics pipeline: agents push metrics into a durable log, a time-series database stores them with rollups, and an alert engine evaluates rules.

Agents or exporters send metrics to ingestion gateways that write to Kafka. Consumers batch-write to a time-series DB sharded by metric and time, with downsampled rollups for long retention. An alert evaluator runs rules on streaming or queried data and sends firing alerts to a notification service (dedup, grouping, silencing, paging). Dashboards query the TSDB through a cache.
Probes: write throughput and cardinality explosion, retention and downsampling, push vs pull collection, alert flapping and dedup, and monitoring the monitoring system itself.

cards.name: Design Typeahead System
back: Precompute top-K suggestions per prefix in a trie (or prefix-to-list store), built offline from query logs and served from memory.

The client sends the typed prefix (debounced) to a suggestion service backed by an in-memory trie or Redis map of prefix to top K completions. Query logs flow through Kafka into aggregation jobs that count frequencies and periodically rebuild and swap the trie. Shard by prefix range; cache results at the browser and CDN.
Probes: freshness vs latency (rebuild frequency, trending queries), shard skew on common prefixes, storing top K at each node vs computing on the fly, personalization, and filtering offensive terms.

cards.name: Design a Comment System
back: Store threaded comments as a tree (parent_id plus path or closure) and load them with cursor pagination and lazy expansion of replies.

A comments table holds id, post_id, parent_id, a materialized path, author, body, and score. The API fetches top-level comments by cursor with a depth limit and loads deeper replies on demand. Votes are queued and aggregated into counters in Redis then flushed to the DB. Shard by post_id; sort by new, top, or hot ranking.
Probes: deep threads and expensive subtree queries, hot posts, vote counter contention, stable pagination while sorting changes, and moderation and deletion of parents with children.

cards.name: Design Twitter
back: Hybrid fan-out: push tweet IDs into followers' timelines on write for normal users, but pull celebrity tweets at read time.

Tweets are written to a sharded store (Snowflake IDs). Fan-out workers consume a queue and push the tweet ID into each follower's timeline list in Redis. Reading the home timeline merges the cached list with recent tweets from followed celebrities, then hydrates tweet bodies. A graph store holds follows; media goes to S3 and CDN; search uses a separate index.
Probes: celebrity fan-out storm, memory cost of timeline caches, fan-out lag and consistency, ranking vs reverse chronological, and hot partitions.

cards.name: Design WhatsApp
back: Persistent websocket connections plus a routing layer that maps users to their connection server, with store-and-forward for offline users.

Clients keep a websocket to a chat gateway, which registers the user's server in a session store (Redis). A message is stored, then forwarded to the recipient's server if online or pushed via APNs and FCM if not; clients ack delivery and read. Offline messages sit in a per-user inbox (Cassandra or similar). Groups fan out per member; media uploads go to object storage and the message carries a link.
Probes: per-conversation ordering with sequence IDs, dedup and idempotent delivery, group fan-out, multi-device sync, connection counts per server, and end-to-end encryption.

cards.name: Design Dropbox
back: Chunk files into blocks with content hashing for dedup and delta sync; keep metadata separate from block storage.

A client watcher splits changed files into blocks (about 4 MB) and hashes them. It asks the metadata service which blocks are missing and uploads only those to object storage. The metadata DB (file tree, versions, block lists, sharded by user) commits the new version. A notification service (long poll or websocket) tells other devices, which fetch the changed blocks.
Probes: conflict resolution (conflicted copies), resumable uploads for big files, cross-user dedup privacy, metadata DB scaling and transactional commits, and sharing permissions.

cards.name: Design YouTube
back: Upload then asynchronous transcoding into many bitrates, served as adaptive bitrate segments through a CDN.

The client uploads with resumable chunked upload to blob storage using a pre-signed URL. A queue triggers a transcoding pipeline that splits the video into segments, encodes multiple resolutions and codecs in parallel, and writes segments plus a manifest (HLS or DASH) to object storage. Metadata lives in a sharded DB with a search index. Playback pulls segments from the CDN, with view counts aggregated through a stream pipeline.
Probes: CDN cost and caching long-tail vs popular videos, transcoding retries and cost, thumbnails, view count consistency, and recommendations as a separate system.

cards.name: Design Uber
back: Geospatial index of live driver locations (geohash, quadtree, or H3) plus a matching service that dispatches without double-booking drivers.

Drivers stream GPS updates every few seconds to a location service that keeps them in an in-memory geo index (Redis GEO or a sharded grid). A rider request goes to a ride service that queries nearby available drivers, ranks by ETA, and offers the trip one driver at a time with a timeout, taking a lock or lease on the driver. Trip state lives in a DB state machine; pricing, ETA, and payment are separate services; Kafka carries events.
Probes: very high write rate of location updates, double dispatch races, surge pricing, sharding by city or region, and keeping driver availability state consistent.

cards.name: Design Google Maps
back: Pre-rendered map tiles served from a CDN, and routing over a road graph made fast with hierarchical preprocessing (contraction hierarchies or A*).

An offline pipeline turns map data into vector or raster tiles by zoom, x, and y, stored in object storage and cached at the CDN. A routing service keeps the partitioned road graph in memory with shortcut edges for long-distance queries. Live traffic from GPS probes is aggregated by a stream pipeline into edge weights for ETA. Geocoding and place search use a separate index.
Probes: graph size and partitioning across regions, traffic freshness vs route stability, tile invalidation on map updates, and rerouting load during navigation.

cards.name: Design TicketMaster
back: Strongly consistent seat inventory with temporary holds, plus a waiting room to absorb flash-sale traffic.

Event search and pages are cached and served from Elasticsearch and a CDN. Selecting a seat creates a hold with a TTL (Redis lock or a DB row marked held with an expiry). Payment confirms and a transaction in the SQL store marks the seat sold with optimistic locking, and expired holds release automatically. A virtual queue throttles how many users enter checkout at once.
Probes: preventing double booking, hot events, payment failure and hold expiry, idempotent payments, bot defense, and strong consistency for inventory vs eventual consistency for browsing.

cards.name: Design Netflix
back: Push video content to edge caches (CDN appliances inside ISPs) ahead of demand and stream it with adaptive bitrate.

Studio content is ingested and encoded into many bitrates and codecs, chunked, and pre-positioned on edge servers during off-peak hours. A playback service authorizes the user and returns a manifest pointing at the best nearby edge; the client switches bitrate with network conditions. Metadata and personalization run as microservices, with recommendations computed offline and cached; watch history streams through Kafka into a wide-column store.
Probes: predicting popularity for cache fill, bandwidth cost, DRM and regional licensing, fallback when an edge is unhealthy, and keeping the control plane separate from the data plane.
